source.title: Gradient Energy Matching for Distributed Asynchronous Gradient Descent

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Reports a large-effective-batch asynchronous training result that qualifies the claim that large batches hurt generalization: GEM retained high test accuracy while the targeted momentum SGD proxy overfit. The comparison changes asynchrony and optimizer behavior along with batch size.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior large-batch generalization work but those cited results are not rows. Dropout is part of the MNIST model setup, not an intervention tested for its effect on generalization.
record.test_reason: The study measures GEM's generalization and compares asynchronous GEM with a synchronous momentum proxy, but does not compare large and small batches under a fixed epoch budget. High accuracy at one effective batch size cannot establish whether increasing batch size causes a penalty or whether GEM removes one.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors conclude that GEM maintains stability and generalizability with many asynchronous workers and report better generalization than the targeted momentum proxy. Their suggestion that staleness favors wider minima is an explanation proposed for future study, not an established mechanism.
record.recipe_differences: GEM rescales asynchronous worker updates to match a synchronous momentum SGD proxy; the paper compares it with that proxy rather than reproducing the original large-batch training method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that increasing asynchronous workers changes GEM's scaling factors and effective batch size; at 100 workers it reports the test-accuracy comparison with the proxy.

fits_no_version.finding: On MNIST, GEM reaches 99.38% test accuracy with 100 asynchronous workers. Figure 5 shows the momentum proxy beginning to overfit while GEM does not.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Asynchronous GEM can maintain high MNIST accuracy and show less overfitting than its targeted synchronous momentum procedure.

record.problems: The test-accuracy result is reported for one high-worker-count setting. The comparison with the momentum SGD proxy does not isolate batch size, and no uncertainty estimate is given for the reported 99.38% accuracy.
record.rows_left_out: No additional applicable results identified. Reported training-loss curves for stability and update efficiency do not measure the held-out generalization gap named by the versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its comparison with natural-label generalization.
Test error as width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Large versus small batch held-out performance at fixed epoch budgets, and whether recipe adaptations remove a measured batch-size penalty.
The effect of adding or removing dropout; dropout is only part of the model setup.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps; the proposed sharp-minima explanation is not measured.
Removing memorized examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No version-specific verdict is warranted. ImageNet results report training loss and update efficiency, not held-out performance. Section 4.1 says its results average three consecutive runs, but supplies no uncertainty estimate for the 99.38% accuracy.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence were not tested.
Width scaling beyond the interpolation threshold was not tested.
Convolutional versus fully connected image generalization was not tested.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under tuning were not tested.

The comparison is between GEM at 100 asynchronous workers and its targeted momentum SGD proxy; it does not isolate batch size under fixed epoch budgets across optimizers, or test the listed recipe adaptations.
Dropout was used in the MNIST network, but its effect on held-out error was not tested.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the generalization gap were not measured.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy was not tested.

rows.subject: GEM
rows.operation_detail: Trained with 100 asynchronous workers; effective batch size B = 100 × 64.
rows.note: The result is for GEM in an asynchronous setting; the paper contrasts it with the targeted momentum SGD proxy, which starts to overfit.
rows.check: The 99.38% test accuracy is correctly reported, but has no small-batch held-out baseline. The stated effective batch size is 6400, while individual asynchronous updates use 64 examples. Each worker contributes one epoch, so increasing workers also increases total data exposure. This is GEM method performance, not a measurement of V5's batch-size penalty.

rows.subject: targeted momentum SGD procedure
rows.operation_detail: Trained as the target synchronous momentum SGD proxy; training and validation losses are plotted.
rows.measure: training and validation loss; authors state that it starts to overfit
rows.note: The text says the proxy starts to overfit; the plotted values are not stated numerically.
rows.check: Figure 5 supports the authors' description of overfitting in the momentum proxy, but compares optimization procedures rather than large versus small batches. Its batch configuration is not specified in the supplied description. The row's partial state cannot be interpreted as evidence of V5.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: MNIST, GEM with 100 asynchronous workers and effective batch size B = 100 × 64, compared with the targeted momentum SGD proxy
reader_labels.reason: GEM reached 99.38% final test accuracy while the proxy started to overfit, qualifying a general large-batch penalty claim in this asynchronous setting (R1, R2).
